title: Before You Change One Line of Code, Understand Its Blast Radius
description: How dependency mapping and connected context help teams reason about the real impact of a software change.
body:
## Small changes can have large consequences
A one-line change can look harmless in a diff. In a connected system, however, the same change may affect APIs, data contracts, business rules, tests, and downstream services.

That is the challenge of blast-radius analysis: understanding what might change beyond the code directly edited.

## Why file-level search is not enough
Text search and symbol references are useful starting points, but they rarely capture the full picture. Runtime integrations, configuration, event consumers and business processes can create relationships that are not obvious from a single file.

Even experienced engineers may need to consult architecture diagrams, tickets, test suites and teammates to assemble the complete story.

## A better change-impact checklist
Before implementing a change, identify the entry point, callers, data inputs and outputs, and any consumers of those outputs. Review relevant tests and documentation. Ask whether the change affects a public contract or an implicit business assumption.

The important distinction is between evidence and confidence. A dependency graph can suggest where to look, but engineers still need to verify runtime behavior and business expectations.

## Connecting code with intent
A useful impact assessment should answer both technical and product questions: which components may be affected, and which user-facing capability relies on them?

Connecting requirements and architecture to code helps make those questions easier to investigate. It also gives reviewers a shared explanation of why the proposed change is safe.

## Where AI can help
AI can assist by summarizing related code, highlighting potential dependencies and assembling a review checklist. Its suggestions should remain inspectable, with links back to source evidence rather than unsupported claims.

Interfluent's connected-engineering-context direction is relevant here: making system relationships easier to navigate before a change is merged.

## Make impact analysis part of the workflow
Start with high-risk changes. Capture the affected components, tests, interfaces and documentation in the pull request. Over time, teams can make the evidence easier to collect and keep current.

A good change review does not merely ask, “Does this code work?” It asks, “What else could this change affect?”
author: Interfluent team
